power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).
#### Packages / Dependencies

#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2106 columns across 165 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 165 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Background: Scrub typhus is a major yet neglected vector-borne disease in Thailand, where it has been nationally notifiable for over two decades.

However, long-term changes in its epidemiology, including reporting proportions, transmission intensity, disease severity, and seasonal patterns, have not been comprehensively characterised at the national level.

We analysed 22 years of national surveillance data for scrub typhus in Thailand (2003-2024) using a latent process model that jointly fits reported cases with published nationwide seroprevalence data and antibody kinetics to estimate reporting proportions and underlying transmission dynamics across all 77 provinces of Thailand.
Findings: Over the 22-year study period, 143096 cases and 119 deaths were reported nationally.
Estimated reporting proportion broadly mirrored transmission intensity, being higher in high-burden regions and lower elsewhere.
Estimated reporting proportion declined synchronously across all regions during the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by rapid rebound by 2024.
After adjusting for estimated reporting, the estimated force of infection was highest in the northern provinces but also substantial in the northeast and south, with upward trends in some provinces.
Susceptibility among older adults aged 65 and above increased progressively over the study period, reversing the pattern observed two decades earlier.

Case-fatality among reported cases in the 25-35-year reference group was low and declined from 0.15% (95% Credible Interval [CrI]: 0.07-0.30%) to 0.06% (95% CrI: 0.02-0.12%), while relative case-fatality among adults above 65 remained elevated across all periods.
Three seasonal patterns, differing mainly in peak timing, were identified and remained largely stable over time.

Conclusion: Over two decades, scrub typhus transmission in Thailand appears to extend well beyond its traditionally recognised northern focus, with estimated substantial burden in regions that have received less attention, while the demographic profile of those most affected has shifted progressively toward older adults.
These findings support the need for regionally tailored surveillance, age-targeted clinical preparedness, and sustained investment in understanding the ecological drivers of transmission.
OpenAI's GPT-5.3 model was used exclusively for language editing to improve the grammar and clarity of the manuscript and for commenting and annotating programming code.
The authors were solely responsible for all scientific aspects of this work, including conceptualisation, study design, data analysis, interpretation of results, and figure generation.
The authors reviewed and take full responsibility for all final content.
Scrub typhus is a common but neglected cause of fever in Thailand, where it has been reported through the national surveillance system for over two decades.
However, trends in reported cases can be misleading because they reflect not only true changes in transmission but also variation in diagnosis and reporting over time and across regions.

We developed a model that combines surveillance data with seroprevalence surveys and antibody kinetics to estimate transmission and reporting jointly, allowing us to estimate how transmission intensity, disease severity, and seasonal patterns have evolved from 2003 to 2024 across all 77 provinces.
Our estimates suggest that substantial transmission occurs not only in the well-studied northern provinces but also in the northeast and south, where the disease has received less attention.
Susceptibility has progressively shifted toward older adults, who also face elevated case-fatality, while three seasonal patterns vary by region and have remained largely stable over time.

These findings suggest that scrub typhus control in Thailand requires a shift from a predominantly northern focus toward regionally tailored strategies that account for local transmission timing, an ageing at-risk population, and the ecological drivers that sustain transmission in each setting.
Scrub typhus remains a neglected vector-borne disease in Thailand, more than seven decades after its first report in the country in 1952 1 .
text.formatted: Scrub typhus remains a neglected vector-borne disease in Thailand, more than seven decades after its first report in the country in 1952 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: The disease is caused by obligate intracellular bacteria of the genus Orientia and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected larval trombiculid mites (Acari: Trombiculidae), commonly known as chiggers.
Infection can lead to severe febrile illness with systemic complications and, if not treated promptly, may result in substantial morbidity and death 2 .
text.formatted: Infection can lead to severe febrile illness with systemic complications and, if not treated promptly, may result in substantial morbidity and death <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Although effective antibiotics are available, misdiagnosis 3, 4 and uneven access to care 5 continue to cause preventable deaths from scrub typhus.
text.formatted: Although effective antibiotics are available, misdiagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> and uneven access to care <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> continue to cause preventable deaths from scrub typhus.

text.text: Understanding how the epidemiology of scrub typhus evolves over the long term is important for assessing disease burden, guiding public health interventions, and identifying emerging trends.

This is particularly relevant for scrub typhus, as the ecology and seasonal activity of its chigger vectors are closely tied to temperature, rainfall, and humidity 6 , while human exposure is shaped by land use, agricultural practices, and demographic shifts.
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant for scrub typhus, as the ecology and seasonal activity of its chigger vectors are closely tied to temperature, rainfall, and humidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , while human exposure is shaped by land use, agricultural practices, and demographic shifts.

text.text: In Thailand, rapid urbanisation, an ageing agricultural workforce, and ongoing environmental change may all be reshaping the transmission landscape, making sustained epidemiological monitoring essential.
Thailand's nationwide passive surveillance system for scrub typhus, operated through the National Disease Surveillance database (R506), provides a valuable resource for such monitoring.

Government and private healthcare facilities across all 77 provinces report clinically suspected and laboratory-confirmed cases, yielding a continuous record of notifications spanning more than two decades.

Using these data from 2003 to 2018, Wangrangsimakul et al. 7 described rising incidence, geographic concentration in the northern region, and associations with agricultural occupation and environmental factors in Chiang Rai Province.
text.formatted: Using these data from 2003 to 2018, Wangrangsimakul et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> described rising incidence, geographic concentration in the northern region, and associations with agricultural occupation and environmental factors in Chiang Rai Province.

text.text: Passive surveillance data, however, do not directly reflect underlying transmission.
Reported case counts are shaped by healthcare-seeking behaviour, diagnostic capacity, clinical awareness, and reporting practices, all of which may vary across regions and over time.

Temporal trends in such data therefore represent a mixture of true epidemiological change and variation in detection and reporting and may be misinterpreted if these processes are not explicitly accounted for.

Several approaches have been proposed to address underreporting and under-ascertainment in infectious disease surveillance, including capture-recapture methods, multiplier approaches, and model-based estimation 8 , each with different data requirements and assumptions.
text.formatted: Several approaches have been proposed to address underreporting and under-ascertainment in infectious disease surveillance, including capture-recapture methods, multiplier approaches, and model-based estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , each with different data requirements and assumptions.

text.text: In this study, we extend the analysis of Wangrangsimakul et al. 7 through 2024 and address the limitations of passive surveillance by jointly modelling reported case data with nationwide seroprevalence data and published antibody kinetics.
text.formatted: In this study, we extend the analysis of Wangrangsimakul et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> through 2024 and address the limitations of passive surveillance by jointly modelling reported case data with nationwide seroprevalence data and published antibody kinetics.

text.text: This approach allows us to estimate temporal changes in reporting and underlying transmission jointly, and to examine long-term shifts over 22 years across four key dimensions: reporting proportions, transmission intensity, disease severity, and seasonal patterns.
Our aim is to characterise how the epidemiology of scrub typhus in Thailand has evolved over this period and to identify priorities for surveillance, research, and public health action.

Scrub typhus reported cases and deaths from 2003 to 2024 were obtained from the National Disease Surveillance (Report 506) database 9 , publicly available passive disease surveillance system by the Division of Epidemiology, Department of Disease Control, Ministry of Public Health (MoPH), Thailand.
text.formatted: Scrub typhus reported cases and deaths from 2003 to 2024 were obtained from the National Disease Surveillance (Report 506) database <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> , publicly available passive disease surveillance system by the Division of Epidemiology, Department of Disease Control, Ministry of Public Health (MoPH), Thailand.

text.text: Reported cases in the database included suspected, probable, and confirmed cases, defined as follows : (1) suspected cases fulfilled the clinical criteria and had a history of environmental exposure; (2) probable cases fulfilled the clinical criteria, had a history of contact with confirmed cases, and met the presumptive laboratory diagnosis criteria, that is an immunochromatographic assay; and (3) confirmed cases fulfilled the clinical criteria and met the laboratory diagnosis criteria, including polymerase chain reaction, indirect immunofluorescent assay, indirect immunoperoxidase test, or Weil Felix test to OX K 10.
text.formatted: Reported cases in the database included suspected, probable, and confirmed cases, defined as follows : (1) suspected cases fulfilled the clinical criteria and had a history of environmental exposure; (2) probable cases fulfilled the clinical criteria, had a history of contact with confirmed cases, and met the presumptive laboratory diagnosis criteria, that is an immunochromatographic assay; and (3) confirmed cases fulfilled the clinical criteria and met the laboratory diagnosis criteria, including polymerase chain reaction, indirect immunofluorescent assay, indirect immunoperoxidase test, or Weil Felix test to OX K <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref>.

text.text: The annual disease surveillance data consist of two sub-datasets describing the epidemiology for the same year: (1) monthly reported scrub typhus cases and deaths; and (2) annual reported scrub typhus cases and deaths by age group.
Data are reported by province, covering all 77 provinces of Thailand across all 13 health regions.

Data on the proportion of scrub typhus sero-positivity were extracted from Gonwong et al., (2022) 11 based on immunoglobulin G (IgG) measurements using ELISA among young men (average age 21 years at the time of measurement) across all provinces of Thailand in 2007-2008 and 2012.
text.formatted: Data on the proportion of scrub typhus sero-positivity were extracted from Gonwong et al., (2022) <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> based on immunoglobulin G (IgG) measurements using ELISA among young men (average age 21 years at the time of measurement) across all provinces of Thailand in 2007-2008 and 2012.

text.text: In this study, sero-positivity was defined using a cutoff of two standard deviations above the mean optical density of negative control sera.
Reported seroprevalence was categorised into the following ranges: 10%, 11-15%, 16-20%, 21-25%, and 26-35%.
Historical annual population sizes by province and age group were obtained from the Administrative Information System of the Bureau of Registration Administration, Ministry of Interior, Thailand 12 .
text.formatted: Historical annual population sizes by province and age group were obtained from the Administrative Information System of the Bureau of Registration Administration, Ministry of Interior, Thailand <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Population data from January of each year were used.

Average annual reported incidence and mortality were calculated as reported cases or deaths divided by person-years (the sum of annual population sizes), per 100,000 and 1,000,000 population, respectively, and were directly age-standardised to the pooled national population (2004-2024) as a sensitivity check.
Ethical approval was not required as this study relied solely on publicly available, deidentified secondary data with no individual-level information.
158 Key quantities used throughout this study are defined in Table 1.
Apart from reported 159 cases, reported deaths and population size, all quantities are model-derived estimates 160 rather than direct observations.

text.text: The term 1 exp ,, therefore represents the probability of infection over the monthly time step, derived from the assumption that infections follow a Poisson process.
The formulation represented in Eq (1) does not imply that the entire population is susceptible to the infection.
Instead, partial immunity, waning protection, and strain turnover are implicitly absorbed into ,, and it should therefore be interpreted as conditional on the existing immune landscape.

In the absence of precise estimates for the Thai population, the clinical fraction was fixed at 0.15 for all age groups, based on the ratio of clinical scrub typhus cases to seroconversion incidence (1238/8123) reported in a recent cohort study in rural India 13.
text.formatted: In the absence of precise estimates for the Thai population, the clinical fraction was fixed at 0.15 for all age groups, based on the ratio of clinical scrub typhus cases to seroconversion incidence (1238/8123) reported in a recent cohort study in rural India <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref>.

text.text: The expected number of reported clinical cases, denoted as + ,, , is modelled by accounting for imperfect surveillance through year-and region-specific reporting proportion , , -0,1., which represents the probability that a true clinical infection is reported by the surveillance system.

Since individual provinces (indexed by ) may report too few cases to reliably estimate their own reporting proportions, provinces are grouped following the 13 MoPH Health Regions (Fig. 1C), and all provinces within the same region share a single reporting proportion:
text.formatted: Since individual provinces (indexed by ) may report too few cases to reliably estimate their own reporting proportions, provinces are grouped following the 13 MoPH Health Regions (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1C</ref>), and all provinces within the same region share a single reporting proportion:

text.text: The reporting proportion is allowed to evolve over time following a region-specific random walk process (Supplementary material Text S1.1), capturing gradual changes in surveillance performance.

In addition, although surveillance relies partly on imperfect diagnostic tests and some false positive reports are therefore expected, these are not modelled explicitly and are instead absorbed into the reporting process and accommodated through the overdispersed observation model.

Model parameters were estimated within a hierarchical Bayesian framework using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling, implemented in Stan via the rstan package.
We assigned weakly informative priors to all parameters to provide broad regularization while allowing the observed data to dominate the posterior distributions (Supplementary material Table S2).

text.text: We ran four independent Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains of 2,000 iterations each, including a 1,000-iteration warm-up period.
Postwarmup, chains were thinned every 4 samples, yielding a total of 1,000 posterior draws.

Convergence and model fit were assessed using trace plots and posterior predictive checks to ensure the model adequately captured the observed temporal trends in scrub typhus reports for each province.

To assess the influence of the fixed clinical fraction () and IgG waning rate (;), we refitted the model with each parameter halved and doubled in turn ( = 0.075 and 0.30; ; = 0.27 and 1.08 year ), keeping all other settings unchanged (Supplementary material Text S4).
Where some chains did not converge, results were summarised from the chains that mixed with each other.

Between 2003 and 2024, a total of 143,096 scrub typhus cases and 119 related deaths were reported.
The five most reported provinces, most of which were located within Health Region 1, were Chiang Rai (17,135), Chiang Mai (16,324), Tak (11,864), Mae Hong Son (11,643), and Nan (9,547) (Fig 1A).
text.formatted: The five most reported provinces, most of which were located within Health Region 1, were Chiang Rai (17,135), Chiang Mai (16,324), Tak (11,864), Mae Hong Son (11,643), and Nan (9,547) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1A</ref>).

text.text: Accounting for population size, these five provinces also had the highest average annual reported incidence, led by Mae Hong Son (195.0 per 100,000 population per year), followed by Tak (88.7), Nan (78.4), Chiang Rai (58.4) and Chiang Mai (40.5).
At the regional level, Health Regions 1 (42%), 9 (11%), 2 (11%), 10 (11%), and 11 (7%) reported the highest cumulative case numbers, respectively.
Relative to population size, reported incidence was highest in Health Regions 1 (42.4 per 100,000), 2 (18.1), 10 (13.1), 9 (9.5) and 11 (8.8), compared with 8.7 per 100,000 nationally.

While cumulative deaths were not concentrated in a single health region (Fig 1B), the highest numbers were reported in Chiang Rai (29), Nakhon Ratchasima (18), Surat Thani (15), Mae Hong Son (9), and Chiang Mai (8).
text.formatted: While cumulative deaths were not concentrated in a single health region (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1B</ref>), the highest numbers were reported in Chiang Rai (29), Nakhon Ratchasima (18), Surat Thani (15), Mae Hong Son (9), and Chiang Mai (8).

text.text: Relative to population size, reported mortality was highest in Mae Hong Son (1.5 per 1,000,000 population per year), Chiang Rai (1.0), Surat Thani (0.6), Phayao (0.3) and Nakhon Ratchasima (0.3).
Direct age standardisation produced nearly identical rankings of provinces (Spearman correlation ≥0.98 for both incidence and mortality).
Scrub typhus cases gradually increased, reaching a peak in 2013, followed by a sharp decline until 2016 and then a subsequent rise.

Extending this temporal trend, our study observed another marked decrease in reported cases during 2020-2021, likely reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on either environmental exposure, health-seeking behaviours, or health system functioning (Fig. 1D).
text.formatted: Extending this temporal trend, our study observed another marked decrease in reported cases during 2020-2021, likely reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on either environmental exposure, health-seeking behaviours, or health system functioning (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1D</ref>).

text.text: A similar effect was evident in mortality data, with no deaths reported in 2021 (Fig. 1E).
text.formatted: A similar effect was evident in mortality data, with no deaths reported in 2021 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1E</ref>).

text.text: Case reporting, however, rebounded rapidly to pre-pandemic levels from 2023 onwards.
Annual reported cases and deaths in 2024 were 8,959 and 7, respectively.
Of the total reported cases, the most affected age cohorts were 45-55 (17%), 35-45 (16%), and 25-35 years (14%) (Fig 1F).
text.formatted: Of the total reported cases, the most affected age cohorts were 45-55 (17%), 35-45 (16%), and 25-35 years (14%) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1F</ref>).

text.text: In contrast, mortality was skewed towards older individuals, with the highest proportion among those aged 65 years and above (23%), followed by the 45-55 (18%) and 55-65 (16%) age groups.

Coupling national surveillance data with seroprevalence data within a hierarchical Bayesian framework enabled estimation of reporting proportion, defined as the proportion of clinical infections reported through the surveillance system, a modelderived latent estimate rather than a directly observed surveillance metric.
Reporting proportion for scrub typhus varied over time between 2003 and 2024 across all 13 Health Regions (2).

During the early 2010s, Health Regions 1 and 2 showed relatively higher reporting proportions than other regions, peaking at 0.89 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 0.75-0.97) in 2013 and 0.84 (95% CrI: 0.69-0.93) in 2010, respectively.
In contrast, Health Regions 4, 5, and 6 consistently exhibited lower reporting proportion, never exceeding 0.40 throughout the observation period.
A notable pattern observed across nearly all regions was a synchronized and marked decline in reporting proportion during 2020-2021 (Fig 2).
text.formatted: A notable pattern observed across nearly all regions was a synchronized and marked decline in reporting proportion during 2020-2021 (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: In Health Region 1, reporting proportion decreased from a pre-pandemic level to 0.26 (95% CrI: 0.19 to 0.34) in 2021.

Such notable reductions were observed in Health Regions 7, 9, 10, and 11, where reporting proportion fell to 0.19 (95% CrI: 0.12 to 0.29), 0.19 (95% CrI: 0.12 to 0.27), 0.20 (95% CrI: 0.12 to 0.32), and 0.33 (95%CrI: 0.24 to 0.44), respectively.
By 2024, all regions showed a rapid rebound in reporting proportion, albeit with some geographical variation.

text.formatted: (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: The spatial distribution map for 2024 indicates that the highest estimated reporting proportions were observed in Health Regions 11, 1, 10, and 7, reaching 0.83 (95% CrI: 0.66 to 0.94), 0.69 (95% CrI: 0.51 to 0.87), 0.62 (95% CrI: 0.37 to 0.87), and 0.59 (95% CrI: 0.37 to 0.82), respectively.

Posterior draws showed a negative relationship between estimated force of infection and reporting proportion within province-years (Figure S1), reflecting their multiplicative contribution to reported cases.
text.formatted: Posterior draws showed a negative relationship between estimated force of infection and reporting proportion within province-years (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>), reflecting their multiplicative contribution to reported cases.

text.text: Most provinces exhibited relatively stable transmission between 2003 and 2024, with average annual FOI (the estimated annual hazard of infection per at-risk person) remaining below 10 per at-risk person-year.

This corresponds to fewer than approximately 100 infections per 100,000 at-risk population per year, including both clinical and subclinical infections, particularly in Health Regions 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: This corresponds to fewer than approximately 100 infections per 100,000 at-risk population per year, including both clinical and subclinical infections, particularly in Health Regions 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: Persistent high-incidence hotspots with a gradual increasing trend were observed in northern and western border provinces, notably Mae Hong Son and Tak, where the estimated annual incidence in 2024 exceeded 1,000 infections per 100,000 at-risk population.

It is worth noting that provinces in Health Regions 9 and 10 have consistently experienced high transmission throughout the observation period, with estimated FOI levels comparable to historically top-reporting provinces such as Chiang Rai, Chiang Mai, and Nan.
Susceptibility to scrub typhus infection showed a strong association with age, particularly in the most recent periods (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: Susceptibility to scrub typhus infection showed a strong association with age, particularly in the most recent periods (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>).

text.text: Individuals younger than the reference age group (25-35 years) consistently exhibited lower susceptibility, with estimated relative susceptibility and 95% CrI remaining below 1.
In contrast, elderly showed notable changes over time.
By 2019-2024, individuals aged over 65 had a relative susceptibility of 1.6 (95% CrI: 1.5 to 1.6), compared with 0.7 (95% CrI: 0.7 to 0.8) in 2003-2007.
Similar upward trends were observed in the 45-55 and 55-65 age groups across the two-decade.

The estimated case-fatality rate among reported cases for the reference group (25-35 years) declined sharply from 0.15% (95% CrI: 0.07-0.30%) in 2003-2007 to 0.06% (95% CrI: 0.02-0.12%) in 2008-2012, after which it remained stable at approximately 0.06-0.07% through 2019-2024.
Estimates of the relative case-fatality rate had substantially wider credible intervals than those for susceptibility, reflecting the smaller number of reported deaths (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: Estimates of the relative case-fatality rate had substantially wider credible intervals than those for susceptibility, reflecting the smaller number of reported deaths (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>).

text.text: Despite this uncertainty, individuals aged over 65 had consistently elevated case-fatality rates relative to the 25-35 year reference group, with posterior mean estimates exceeding 1.0 across all time periods and ranking among the highest of all age groups, although credible intervals overlapped 1 for most age groups.

Combined with the patterns observed for relative susceptibility, these findings suggest that clinical infection has become increasingly concentrated among older populations over time, a group that also faces elevated mortality risk.
Rather than characterising seasonal patterns by administrative regions as in a previous studiy 7 , we classified seasonality at the period-province level.
Using _-means clustering, we identified three distinct seasonal patterns, distinguished by their peak timing and peak-to-trough amplitude (Fig. 5).
text.formatted: Using _-means clustering, we identified three distinct seasonal patterns, distinguished by their peak timing and peak-to-trough amplitude (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>).

text.text: The patterns were distinguished mainly by peak timing.
Pattern 1 had a late-September peak and the highest amplitude ratio (3.1).
Pattern 2 peaked in early July with a moderate amplitude ratio (2.2).
Pattern 3, by contrast, exhibited relatively flat seasonality, peaking earlier in the year with the lowest amplitude ratio (1.9).
The 2019-2024 map illustrates the geographic distribution of seasonal patterns (Fig. 5), which remained broadly stable across all periods.
text.formatted: The 2019-2024 map illustrates the geographic distribution of seasonal patterns (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>), which remained broadly stable across all periods.

text.text: Pattern 1 was the most widespread, covering 52% of provinces, primarily across the Northeast and Central regions.
Pattern 2 accounted for 38%, concentrated in the North, including the western border provinces, and the South.
Pattern 3 represented a small but persistent share (10%), scattered across the South, East and Central regions.
This stability was further reflected by the fact that 58% of provinces retained the same seasonal pattern throughout the entire observation period.
When uncertainty in the estimated seasonal curves was considered, this proportion was 44% (95% CrI: 32-55%).
Assignment to Pattern 3 was the least certain, reflecting its flatter seasonal profile.

Characterising how the epidemiology of a disease evolves over the long term is essential for assessing disease burden, guiding public health interventions, and understanding how the disease interacts with environmental and socio-economic changes, including those driven by climate.

A previous study analysed nationwide passive surveillance data for scrub typhus in Thailand from 2003 to 2018, focusing on broad historical characteristics of the disease while restricting temporal trend analysis to a single province without assessing changes at the national level 7 .
text.formatted: A previous study analysed nationwide passive surveillance data for scrub typhus in Thailand from 2003 to 2018, focusing on broad historical characteristics of the disease while restricting temporal trend analysis to a single province without assessing changes at the national level <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: The present study extends these data through 2024 and examines long-term shifts over 22 years across four key aspects: (1) reporting proportions, (2) transmission intensity, (3) disease severity, and (4) seasonal patterns.
Long-term national surveillance systems offer a valuable opportunity to examine how the epidemiology of notifiable diseases evolves over space and time.

In Thailand, data from the National Disease Surveillance database (R506) have been widely used to describe disease dynamics [18] [19] [20] [21] and, in some cases, to explore correlations with environmental variables.
text.formatted: In Thailand, data from the National Disease Surveillance database (R506) have been widely used to describe disease dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> and, in some cases, to explore correlations with environmental variables.

text.text: However, surveillance data are inherently imperfect and do not directly reflect underlying transmission.

Reported incidence is shaped by the reporting proportion, which depends on diagnostic capacity, healthcare access, surveillance practices, diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, and clinical awareness.

Temporal trends in these data therefore reflect a mixture of true epidemiological change and variation in detection and reporting, and may be misinterpreted if these processes are not explicitly accounted for.
To address this, we integrated passive surveillance data with nationwide seroprevalence data and antibody kinetics to jointly infer reporting proportions and underlying transmission intensity.
Clinical attention to scrub typhus may have influenced case reporting.

Estimated reporting proportion generally mirrored the transmission intensity across regions, with higher FOI in Health Regions 1 and 2 possibly leading clinicians to consider the disease more consistently in the differential diagnosis of undifferentiated febrile illness, thereby contributing to higher detection.

By contrast, regions with lower FOI, including Health Regions 4, 5, and 6, may have given the disease less diagnostic consideration, partly explaining their lower reporting proportions due to under-diagnosis 8, 22 .
text.formatted: By contrast, regions with lower FOI, including Health Regions 4, 5, and 6, may have given the disease less diagnostic consideration, partly explaining their lower reporting proportions due to under-diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Beyond these regional differences, the diversion of healthcare resources during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021) coincided with a temporary synchronised decline in reporting proportion.

Nevertheless, the rapid rebound to near pre-pandemic levels by 2024 in most regions suggests a resilient surveillance infrastructure, likely supported by Thailand's well-established public health system and its capacity to restore routine disease detection after major systemic disruptions.

Because the reporting proportion also absorbs changes in diagnostic practice, including the gradual replacement of the Weil-Felix test by more specific assays, its temporal trends should be interpreted as the combined effect of clinical awareness, healthcare access and diagnostic performance rather than of any single factor.

After accounting for temporal variation in reporting proportions, the estimated force of infection suggested substantial geographic heterogeneity in transmission, which may reflect ecological and occupational factors such as climate, land use, and exposure to chigger habitats.

Health Regions 1 and 2 in the north consistently exhibited the highest FOI, with Chiang Rai, Chiang Mai, and Nan long recognised as high-burden provinces and the setting for much of the existing field and clinical research [23] [24] [25] .
text.formatted: Health Regions 1 and 2 in the north consistently exhibited the highest FOI, with Chiang Rai, Chiang Mai, and Nan long recognised as high-burden provinces and the setting for much of the existing field and clinical research <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> .

text.text: Our estimates further highlight that Mae Hong Son and Tak, which have smaller populations and consequently lower absolute case counts, harbour FOI at least as high as these betterstudied provinces, with both showing notable upward trends, particularly Mae Hong Son.

This reinforces earlier findings by 7 , who reported that Mae Hong Son and Tak had the highest incidence rates among all Thai provinces, and suggests that these areas may benefit from increased research and public health attention.
text.formatted: This reinforces earlier findings by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , who reported that Mae Hong Son and Tak had the highest incidence rates among all Thai provinces, and suggests that these areas may benefit from increased research and public health attention.

text.text: Beyond the north, the northeastern regions (Health Regions 8-10) showed moderate but sustained FOI, while the southern regions (Health Regions 11 and 12) displayed considerable within-region heterogeneity, with Ranong in particular showing a notable rise over the study period.

These observations suggest that scrub typhus transmission in Thailand extends well beyond the mountainous terrain and ethnic minority populations where the disease has traditionally been focused 5, 26.
text.formatted: These observations suggest that scrub typhus transmission in Thailand extends well beyond the mountainous terrain and ethnic minority populations where the disease has traditionally been focused <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref>.

text.text: Estimated age-specific susceptibility to scrub typhus showed a temporal shift over the study period.
In 2003-2007, susceptibility was relatively uniform across adult age groups, with older adults even showing lower values than the 25-35-year reference group.
By 2019-2024, however, this pattern had reversed, with adults aged 55 and above showing the highest relative susceptibility.
Children remained consistently less susceptible than adults throughout.

This shift may reflect Thailand's rapidly ageing agricultural workforce, in which older farmers continue to maintain exposure to chigger habitats while younger cohorts increasingly move into less exposed occupations or urban settings 27, 28 .
text.formatted: This shift may reflect Thailand's rapidly ageing agricultural workforce, in which older farmers continue to maintain exposure to chigger habitats while younger cohorts increasingly move into less exposed occupations or urban settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Although cumulative lifetime exposure in older adults could contribute to higher background seropositivity and potential false positive diagnoses 29 , this alone is unlikely to explain the observed temporal shift, as such an effect would be expected to remain constant across periods rather than progressively increase.
text.formatted: Although cumulative lifetime exposure in older adults could contribute to higher background seropositivity and potential false positive diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , this alone is unlikely to explain the observed temporal shift, as such an effect would be expected to remain constant across periods rather than progressively increase.

text.text: In absolute terms, case-fatality remained low throughout the study period and declined over the first decade before stabilising.

This may reflect the expansion of Thailand's Universal Coverage Scheme from 2002, which substantially improved healthcare access in rural areas where scrub typhus burden is highest 30 , enabling earlier presentation and more timely diagnosis and treatment.
text.formatted: This may reflect the expansion of Thailand's Universal Coverage Scheme from 2002, which substantially improved healthcare access in rural areas where scrub typhus burden is highest <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , enabling earlier presentation and more timely diagnosis and treatment.

text.text: The relative case-fatality rate, however, was consistently elevated among adults above 65 across all periods, albeit with wide credible intervals, consistent with findings across endemic settings linking older age to higher complication rates, immunosenescence, and comorbidities [31] [32] [33] .
text.formatted: The relative case-fatality rate, however, was consistently elevated among adults above 65 across all periods, albeit with wide credible intervals, consistent with findings across endemic settings linking older age to higher complication rates, immunosenescence, and comorbidities <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> .

text.text: As Thailand's population continues to age, the combination of rising susceptibility and persistently elevated case-fatality among older adults underscores the need for targeted clinical vigilance and public health efforts in ageing rural communities.
Three seasonal patterns of scrub typhus transmission, differing mainly in peak timing, were identified across Thailand through 2003 to 2024.
Pattern 1, the most common at the provincial level, showed strong seasonality peaking in late September (amplitude ratio 3.1), coinciding with the latter part of the monsoon season.
Pattern 2 peaked earlier around July (amplitude ratio 2.2), while Pattern 3 showed minimal seasonal variation (amplitude ratio 1.9), suggesting near year-round transmission.

Although Pattern 1 covered the majority of provinces, the national-level seasonal profile more closely resembles Pattern 2, reflecting the disproportionate contribution of highincidence provinces that follow this earlier-peaking pattern.

These patterns remained relatively stable over the two decades of the study period, with no clear directional shift between periods, suggesting that the underlying drivers of seasonality have not fundamentally changed; the shifts observed in a minority of provinces should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainty in pattern assignment, and seasonality appears to be shaped largely by relatively fixed climatic and geographic factors.

In addition, while our analysis identified distinct seasonal patterns and tracked their longitudinal shifts across provinces, we did not formally investigate the role of large-scale climate variability such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) in shaping these patterns.
Linking annual transmission intensity at the national level to climate indices is an important next step that could help clarify the mechanisms driving observed inter-annual variability.
This subnational heterogeneity in seasonal timing is not unique to Thailand.

In China, three epidemiologically distinct regions with markedly different seasonal profiles have been identified: a sharp October-November peak in the middle-eastern provinces, a broader June-September peak in the southwest, and a more extended transmission season in the southeast 34 .
text.formatted: In China, three epidemiologically distinct regions with markedly different seasonal profiles have been identified: a sharp October-November peak in the middle-eastern provinces, a broader June-September peak in the southwest, and a more extended transmission season in the southeast <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: In South Korea, cases concentrate in October-November but the peak shifts to later months at lower latitudes 35 , while Japan shows a bimodal pattern in the north with peaks in both May and October-November, compared to a single dominant October-November peak in the south 36 .
text.formatted: In South Korea, cases concentrate in October-November but the peak shifts to later months at lower latitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> , while Japan shows a bimodal pattern in the north with peaks in both May and October-November, compared to a single dominant October-November peak in the south <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> .

text.text: In India, peak timing varies regionally: from August to February with an October peak in the south, and broadly July to November in the north and northeast 37 .
text.formatted: In India, peak timing varies regionally: from August to February with an October peak in the south, and broadly July to November in the north and northeast <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Thailand's Pattern 3, with its near year-round transmission in the south, echoes the extended seasons seen in equatorial parts of Southeast China and Yunnan, where year-round rainfall likely sustains more constant mite populations.

Taken together, these comparisons suggest that scrub typhus seasonality is shaped by the interplay of mite species composition, host population dynamics, human exposure patterns linked to agricultural calendars and land use, and abiotic conditions that influence all of these simultaneously.

Predicting case reports directly from climate data alone, as several studies have attempted, has therefore limitations, not only because climate acts indirectly through these intermediary pathways, but also because reported case counts are further filtered through healthcare-seeking behaviour, diagnostic practices, and reporting systems that may themselves vary seasonally.

Given this complexity, effective control measures, whether through targeted vector management, seasonally timed risk communication and prevention, or clinical preparedness, need to be locally tailored to the specific drivers of transmission in each setting.
This requires disentangling the contributions of each of these interacting factors, yet several critical data gaps remain to be addressed.
Despite Thailand being a major endemic setting, its chigger vector ecology remains largely unexplored.

More than 20 Leptotrombidium species have been reported from Thailand 38 , and O. tsutsugamushi has been recently detected in chiggers from multiple genera beyond Leptotrombidium 23 , yet vector competence, geographic distribution, and seasonal activity have been studied for only a handful of species, mostly in the northern provinces and only for short periods.

text.text: Whether the distinct seasonal patterns identified in our study correspond to different dominant vector species, as demonstrated in Japan, South Korea, and China 35, 36, 39 , or instead reflect regional differences in agricultural calendars and human exposure, remains an open question.

text.text: Beyond vector ecology, important gaps remain in our understanding of rodent host dynamics and their overlap with infected vectors, and occupational and behavioural exposure patterns across regions.
Mathematical modelling frameworks that integrate vector, host, and human data could help translate these observations into locally appropriate strategies.
Realising this will require sustained and standardised surveillance across all three dimensions, both to inform intervention design and to evaluate effectiveness over time.
As with any modelling study that relies on passively collected surveillance data, our approach is subject to certain limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings.
First, baseline force of infection and reporting proportions were estimated jointly and cannot be fully separated using surveillance data alone, since reported cases depend on both.
The model better identifies relative spatial differences because reporting proportion varies by region, whereas transmission varies by province.
Seroprevalence data anchor the overall level only in 2007, 2008 and 2012; otherwise, separation relies on gradually changing reporting.
We therefore interpret spatial patterns and relative differences more confidently than absolute estimates.
The 2020-2021 decline in reported cases is robust, but its attribution to reduced detection versus reduced transmission remains uncertain.

Second, some model parameters, such as antibody kinetics and the clinical fraction, were informed by published literature rather than estimated directly from the data, and may not fully reflect the local epidemiological context in Thailand.
We assessed the influence of these assumptions by refitting the model with each parameter halved and doubled (Supplementary material Text S4; Figures S3-S5).
text.formatted: We assessed the influence of these assumptions by refitting the model with each parameter halved and doubled (Supplementary material Text S4; Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">S3-S5</ref>).

text.text: Doubling the clinical fraction halved the estimated force of infection but left the ranking of provinces, reporting proportions, age-specific susceptibility and casefatality estimates essentially unchanged, and halving the waning rate had a negligible effect.
With a halved clinical fraction, two of four chains did not converge and were excluded, and the remaining chains showed the same pattern with an approximately doubled force of infection.

With a doubled waning rate, no two chains converged, and the most consistent chains implied implausibly intense transmission and very low reporting proportions, suggesting that such rapid antibody waning is difficult to reconcile with the observed data.
Because these parameters scale the relationship between infections and reported cases, they affect absolute estimates more than relative comparisons between provinces or age groups.

Third, the model assumed uniform antibody dynamics across age groups, without accounting for potential age-specific differences in serological response, such as slower antibody decay or higher baseline titres in older adults with repeated lifetime exposure.
Incorporating age-specific serodynamics could refine estimates of susceptibility and help distinguish genuine changes in exposure from diagnostic artefacts.

A further consideration is that the seroprevalence data used for calibration were collected from young men, whose exposure patterns are unlikely to be representative of children, women or older adults; age-specific estimates outside this range therefore depend more heavily on the model structure than on direct serological observation.

Although the serological data were linked to the 15-25-year age group, the model does not distinguish between sexes; if young men are more exposed than young women, as is plausible given occupational and outdoor activities, the estimated force of infection may be overestimated and reporting proportions correspondingly underestimated.

Fourth, the model did not explicitly estimate false positive rates; in endemic settings, background seropositivity from past infections can lead to misclassification, particularly among older adults with cumulative lifetime exposure, potentially inflating apparent susceptibility in these age groups.

Fifth, age-specific susceptibility and case-fatality were estimated at the national level and did not explore regional variation, which may be substantial given the geographic heterogeneity in transmission intensity, bacterial strains, occupational structure, and healthcare access observed across Thailand.

Sixth, surveillance case definitions combined suspected, probable and confirmed cases, and diagnostic practice shifted over the study period from serological methods with limited specificity towards more specific assays.
The aggregated data did not record case classification or the diagnostic test used, precluding their inclusion as covariates in the reporting model.
Changes in diagnostic practice may therefore contribute to the estimated temporal trends in reporting, which we could not separate from changes in healthcare-seeking or surveillance capacity.

However, because the reporting proportion is shared by provinces within each health region, region-wide changes in diagnostic practice cannot explain the contrasting transmission trends observed among provinces within the same region, such as Phatthalung and Narathiwat in Health Region 12, although differences in diagnostic practice between provinces could.

Finally, case-fatality estimates are conditional on reported cases and therefore reflect outcomes among individuals who sought healthcare and received a diagnosis, rather than among all infected individuals; if healthcare-seeking behaviour or diagnostic sensitivity varies by age or region, the estimated rates may not be representative of the true infection fatality.

In conclusion, our model-based estimates suggest that scrub typhus transmission in Thailand is not confined to the north, and that the northeastern and southern regions may represent substantial and under-recognised foci, with estimated force of infection rising in several provinces.

While passive surveillance data are inherently shaped by reporting practices that vary across regions and time, Thailand's long-standing national surveillance infrastructure provides a valuable resource for tracking the evolving epidemiology of scrub typhus when these biases are explicitly modelled and estimates are interpreted in light of their assumptions.
The disease burden is increasingly concentrated among older adults, who show both rising susceptibility and elevated case-fatality.
Seasonal timing of transmission varies markedly across regions but has remained largely stable over two decades.

Together, these findings highlight the need to broaden surveillance and research to underserved endemic areas, direct clinical awareness and public health efforts toward ageing rural populations, and design interventions informed by the distinct seasonal and ecological conditions of each region.
This will require deeper understanding of the interacting vector, host, and human drivers that shape transmission locally.
